query: How does ELBO-based variational inference with inducing points bias posterior contraction rates and boundary recovery, and what conditions make that bias asymptotically negligible?

response.query: How does ELBO-based variational inference with inducing points bias posterior contraction rates and boundary recovery, and what conditions make that bias asymptotically negligible?
response.answer: ELBO-based variational inference uses inducing points to approximate posterior distributions, which can introduce bias but this bias diminishes as the number of inducing points increases. The bias is often negligible in large datasets or when the inducing points are well-chosen.

results.title: The ELBO in Variational Inference
results.content: # The ELBO in Variational Inference. #### I derive the evidence lower bound (ELBO) in variational inference and explore its relationship to the objective in expectation–maximization and the variational autoencoder. In Bayesian inference, we are often interested in the posterior distribution p(Z∣X) where X are our observations, {x1​,…,xN​} and Z are latent variables, {z1​,…,zN​}. However, in many practical models of interest, this posterior is intractable because we cannot compute the evidence or denominator of Bayes’ theorem, p(X). The main idea of variational inference (VI) is to use optimization to find a simpler or more tractable distribution q(Z) from a family of distributions Q such that it is close to the desired posterior distribution p(Z∣X) (Figure 1). In VI, we define “close to” using the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. See my previous post on the KL divergence for a discussion. VI starts with some initial distribution q(0)(Z)∈Q and then iteratively minimizes the KL divergence between the approximating distribution at iteration t, call this q(t)(Z), and the desired posterior p(Z∣X). The goal is to find an optimal distribution q∗(Z) where optimality is defined as having the smallest possible KL divergence between q∗(Z) and p(Z∣X). The main challenge with the variational inference objective in Eq. 1 is that it implicitly depends on the evidence, p(X). DKL​[q(Z)∥p(Z∣X)]​=∫q​q(Z)logp(Z∣X)q(Z)​=Eq(Z)​[logp(Z∣X)q(Z)​]=−ELBO(q)Eq(Z)​[logq(Z)]−Eq(Z)​[logp(Z,X)]​​+logp(X).​(2). Because we cannot compute the desired KL divergence, we optimize a different objective that is equivalent to this KL divergence up to constant. This new objective is called the *evidence lower bound* or ELBO:. ELBO(q):=Eq(Z)​[logp(Z,X)]−Eq(Z)​[logq(Z)].(3). logp(X)=ELBO(q)+DKL​[q(Z)∥p(Z∣X)].(4). In other words, the log evidence logp(X), a fixed quantity for any set of observations X, cannot be less than the ELBO. So if we maximize the ELBO, we minimize the desired KL divergence. EM maximizes the expected log likelihood when q(Z)=p(Z∣X), i.e. logp(X)=∣∣∣∣​ELBO(q)​EM maximizes this​+∣∣∣∣​KL[q(Z)∥p(Z∣X)]​Since this is zero​.(6). VI is a framework, and there are a variety of different ways to optimize this ELBO. (See (Blei et al., 2017) for a much deeper discussion.) A popular approach in deep generative modeling is to use gradient-based optimization of the ELBO. The most famous example of gradient-based VI is probably the *variational autoencoder*.

results.title: Variational Inference and Expectation Maximization – Syed Ashar Javed – Learning to learn
results.content: * p(X) or q(X) denotes probability distribution over the variables X. **E step**: Estimate the latent variables according to posterior distribution calculated with the model parameters. **E step**: Estimate \(Q(\theta, \theta\_t)\) for iteration \(t\). $$Q(\theta, \theta\_t) = \mathbb E\_{p(Z \mid X)}[\log p(X,Z;\theta)]$$. and the probability distribution \(p\) is parameterized by \(\theta\), ie \(\theta\) is the model parameter. Instead, what VI does is replace the intractable distribution, \(p(Z \mid X;\theta)\) by a proxy distribution, \(q(Z)\) and perform inference on it. $$ \begin{align} \log(p(X)) & = \log(\int\_Z \frac{p(X,Z) q(Z)}{q(Z)})\\ & = \log(\mathbb E\_{q(Z)}[\frac{p(X,Z)}{q(Z)}]) \end{align} $$. Finally, coming back to our original problem of minimizing the KL divergence, we can see that since the second term on the RHS of equation \(3\) is independent of \(q\), minimizing the KL divergence is the same as maximizing the ELBO. Furthermore, we also have seen that the log probability of the data has a lower bound called ELBO and the gap between them is quantified by the KL divergence term between the approximating distribution and the original posterior. So, variational inference is all about changing the posterior estimation problem to an optimization problem, namely the maximization of ELBO. $$ELBO(q,\theta) = E\_{q(Z)}[\log(p(X,Z;\theta)] - E\_{q(Z)}[\log(q(Z))]\tag{4}$$. The ELBO in fact is a function of the probability distribution \(q\) and model parameters \(\theta\). The EM algorithm described in the beginning can be interpreted as an iterative algorithm of optimizing \(ELBO(q,\theta)\), keeping one parameter constant at a time. This step does coordinate ascent on \(ELBO(q,\theta\_t)\) at iteration \(t\). Since we know that the optimal \(q\) for the above problem will occur when the approximate distribution equals the original posterior, the solution to the above problem trivially becomes. Note that this step is the same as estimating the function \(Q(\theta,\theta\_t)\) as done in the E-step of EM described above. $$\mathop{\arg\,\max}\limits\_\theta (E\_{p(Z \mid X)}[\log(p(X,Z;\theta)] - E\_{p(Z \mid X)}[\log(p(Z \mid X))])$$. Since the second expectation term is independent of \(\theta\), the problem simplifies to the original M-step of the EM algorithm as described above. $$\mathop{\arg\,\max}\limits\_\theta (E\_{p(Z \mid X)}[\log(p(X,Z;\theta)])$$. The above analysis shows that variational inference is expectation maximization when the variational distribution of VI is the same as the original posterior distribution.

results.title: Variational Inference in Bayesian Neural Networks - GeeksforGeeks
results.content: # Variational Inference in Bayesian Neural Networks Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) extend traditional neural networks by treating weights as probability distributions rather than fixed values. Variational Inference (VI) provides a scalable method to approximate the intractable posterior distribution of these weights. * ****Bayesian Neural Networks:**** Each weight is treated as a probability distribution, representing uncertainty about its true value. ### ****Why Use Variational Inference?**** * ****Challenge:**** Computing the exact "posterior" distribution over all weights (what we believe about weights after seeing the data) is mathematically intractable for neural networks. ## ****How Does Variational Inference Work in BNNs?**** ****Choose a Simple Distribution:**** Pick a family of distributions (e.g., diagonal Gaussian) to approximate the true posterior over weights. ****Optimization Objective:**** Instead of maximizing likelihood (as in standard neural nets), VI maximizes a new objective that balances two things: * ****Fit to Data:**** How well the network explains the observed data (like usual training). ****Gradient-Based Training:**** VI uses gradient descent, just like regular neural networks, but updates both the means and standard deviations of the weight distributions. ****Prediction:**** At test time, predictions are made by averaging over several samples of weights from the learned distribution, capturing model uncertainty. ## Practical Implementation of Variational Inference in BNNs ### ****Main Formula (ELBO)**** > ELBO=Eq(θ)​[logp(data∣θ)]−KL(q(θ)∥p(θ)) * q(θ) : The variational (approximate) posterior distribution over the network weights θ (what we’re learning). * p(data∣θ) : The likelihood how likely the observed data is, given weights θ (model fit). * p(θ) : The prior distribution over weights (our initial belief, e.g., a standard normal distribution). ### ****Practical Training Steps**** Choose Priors and Variational Family****: Set p(θ) (e.g., N(0,1) for each weight). ## results.content: Amortised inference addresses this by learning a single **inference network** that maps an input **x** directly to the parameters of the approximate posterior, so the variational objective becomes: This approach *amortises* the cost of inference over all data points, allowing us to efficiently infer latent variables without having to optimise variational parameters independently for each datapoint. * **Inference network**, often called the “encoder”, which gives us an amortised approximation to the (intractable) true posterior p(z | x) that tells us how to infer latents **z** from data **x**. Te gradients with respect to the generative parameters θ are standard to compute; the challenge lies in differentiating the ELBO with respect to the variational parameters φ, as the expectation is taken over q\_φ(z|x).
